Introduction I’m a software engineer at TSC (Techo Startup Center), and since September 2026 I’ve been building CamWallet v2. CamWallet is a platform that helps government benefit schemes deliver value to the people they’re meant for, and lets those people spend it with approved merchants.
This post explains what v2 changes and why it helps scheme owners, beneficiaries and merchants. It walks through the ledger design that makes the money auditable, and it ends with what I learned from building the epics with an unattended AI agent loop. Engineers working on payments or wallets should get the most from the ledger section. Teams trying AI-assisted development should get the most from the last two sections.
What v2 changes, and why it matters Version 1 worked in four steps.
A scheme defined eligibility rules, and CamWallet decided who qualified. People who qualified received value in a wallet. They paid merchants through a bank, using Bakong, ABA or ACLEDA. The bank confirmed the payment, and CamWallet recorded the outcome. Version 2 changes the first and third steps. The scheme owner decides who qualifies in their own system, and CamWallet records that decision without re-checking it. Payment happens inside CamWallet, from a beneficiary’s grant to a merchant’s balance, with no bank in the path. The ledger, CamDigiKey login, disbursement scheduling, idempotency and audit trail all carry over, so v2 is a milestone on the existing codebase rather than a rewrite.
Those two changes give each group something concrete.
Scheme owners keep control of eligibility, which is their policy decision anyway. CamWallet makes sure the money is spent only with approved merchants, and it tells the owner exactly what to pay each merchant at settlement. Beneficiaries pay by scanning a merchant’s QR in the CamDigiKey app, the national digital identity app they already use. The payment completes immediately, and a declined payment always records one specific reason. Merchants see each payment arrive in the Merchant App and know exactly what each scheme owes them. A merchant with several counters can print a labelled QR for each one. Auditors and finance teams can reconcile every scheme with one balance check instead of investigating transactions by hand. The project delivers a working pilot without waiting for a bank integration. Removing the bank also removed the payment-gateway clients, the eligibility engine and the registry lookup. For a four-week build at pilot volume, Postgres replaced most of the Postgres, MinIO and Kafka stack in the original proposal. The ledger Everything is a transfer between two accounts. Entries are appended and never changed, and replaying an account’s entries explains its balance. That turns reconciliation into arithmetic.
Account What it holds scheme:{id}:expenditure Total ever granted in the scheme grant:{id} One grant’s unspent value payable:{scheme}:{merchant} What the scheme owes one merchant scheme:{id}:paid_out Total recorded as paid to merchants scheme:{id}:returned Unspent value from expired grants Each enrolment is a grant with its own amount and validity dates, and a beneficiary can hold several. A wallet isn’t an account. It is the set of a beneficiary’s grants in one scheme, and its spendable balance counts only grants that are valid today. Payables are kept per scheme, so a merchant serving two schemes has two payables that settle separately.
Operation From → To Disburse scheme expenditure → grant Pay grant (soonest end date first) → payable Record payout payable → scheme paid_out Return expired value grant → scheme returned Expenditure moves only on disbursement, so each scheme satisfies one identity that we check in a single query and assert in a test.
granted = Σ grant balances + Σ payables + paid_out + returned Keeping it correct in Postgres With no bank involved, a payment is one ACID transaction in one database. It needs no distributed transaction and no compensating action. A few rules protect the ledger.
Entries are immutable. A trigger rejects UPDATE and DELETE on ledger entries, so a correction is always a new reversing entry. Cached balances change atomically. Grant and payable balances are cached for payment checks. They change only inside one posting method, through SET balance = balance + :delta, never through a read-modify-write in Java. A test asserts that each cached balance equals the sum of its entries. Every transfer balances. The posting code rejects an unbalanced set of entries before writing. Locks guard the checks. A payment locks the beneficiary’s wallet row before reading any grant, and a dynamic QR is locked first so it can’t be paid twice. Money is exact. Amounts are numeric(19,4) and always carry a currency, and a posting across two currencies is rejected. Each declined payment carries exactly one code from a fixed list, such as QR_EXPIRED, MERCHANT_NOT_PARTICIPATING, CREDIT_EXPIRED or INSUFFICIENT_BALANCE. Reports can group declines by reason from day one, and adding a code later is cheap.
Building it with an AI agent loop I implemented the v2 epics with the BMad Method and bmad-loop, a CLI that runs the implementation phase unattended. It picks a story, writes a spec, implements it, runs a compile-and-typecheck gate and moves on. I held retrospectives after Epic 1 (merchant management) and Epic 3 (scheme participation), and both found the same pattern.
In Epic 1 the loop built all seven stories, plus seven capabilities the pilot didn’t need, including member management, server-side paging and an idempotency key. Human review removed them. The feature commit was about 2,500 lines, and the net change after the slim-down was about 550. The loop’s own review step never triggered, so every defect was found by a person.
Epic 3 was smaller and still left about 250 lines on dev that didn’t survive. The plan said to build a JSON deserializer that dev already had, and the agent followed the plan. A rule to write minimal tests was overshot at first, and then the trim cut the only tests that checked membership and roles.
The code compiled and the tests passed in both epics. The cost came from building the wrong amount of the right thing. The loop is good at matching a plan, but it doesn’t notice when the plan has gone stale or asks for more than the pilot needs.
What you can take from this These are the lessons I’d pass on to anyone building something similar.
Look for the one or two assumptions that drive the design. Writing v2 down as two changed steps out of four made every later decision easier to test. If a proposal followed from neither change, it usually belonged in a later phase. Keep money movements inside one database when you can. A single transaction removes the hardest failure cases in payments. Make the ledger append-only and prove it balances. An immutable entry table plus one reconciliation identity gives auditors a check they can run themselves. Use a closed list of decline reasons. It costs nothing at the start and saves a painful clean-up later. With an agent loop, do the judgement work before the run. Write down each story’s pilot scope and deferrals, check the plan against the current branch, and name the tests that protect something real, such as tenancy and roles, instead of setting a test count. Keep a human review gate on purpose. In both epics, every real defect was found in human review.
summary: How CamWallet v2 lets government schemes pay beneficiaries and merchants in real time without a bank integration, why a double-entry ledger makes it auditable, and what building it with an AI agent loop taught me.
title: CamWallet v2: Benefit Payments on a Closed Ledger

Introduction I’m a software engineer at TSC (Techo Startup Center), and for most of 2026 I’ve worked on ESB-MOT, the Ministry of Tourism’s online licensing platform. This post covers what the platform does, why it matters to the people who use it, how it works underneath, and what I would do differently.
I wrote it for three kinds of reader. Engineers joining a government microservices project will find the architecture walk-through and the testing lessons useful. People planning digital public services will find the section on value. Anyone curious about how a restaurant licence gets issued in Cambodia today can read it from the top.
What ESB is, and what it changes ESB stands for E-Services for Business. It is a Royal Government of Cambodia programme that gives ministries a shared foundation for digital public services. Most licensing follows the same path. A business applies, an officer reviews, the business pays, and the ministry issues a certificate. TSC maintains an open generic template for that path, and each ministry runs its own instance. MOT is the tourism instance, and its first licences cover restaurants, accommodation, sport venues and tour agents.
The value shows up for three groups.
Businesses apply, pay and track their application online instead of visiting an office and carrying paper between desks. Each licence’s fee follows a published schedule. For restaurants, the seating-capacity band is the fee line item, so the owner sees the price before submitting. The ministry gets one backoffice where officers review applications in department-scoped queues. Renewal rules and late penalties are configuration that staff can edit, so a policy change doesn’t need a developer. The public can trust the certificate. The official tourism licence carries a verification QR, and scanning it through verify.gov confirms the licence is genuine. A dedicated service batches payments to the national treasury system (NRMIS), so revenue can reconcile without manual re-entry once that service is deployed. The template also saves effort across government. Each ministry adapts a working platform instead of commissioning its own from scratch. MOT itself was forked from the agriculture ministry’s instance, and the code still carries farm-licence names like FarmType. That cost is real, but it is much smaller than starting over.
How one licence moves through the system The platform is about twenty independent repos. They contain two Nuxt portals (one for the public, one for the backoffice), Spring Boot services, two Spring Cloud Gateways, shared libraries and infrastructure. Services talk mostly through Avro messages on Kafka.
A new restaurant licence passes through five services.
restaurant form (public portal) → Nitro proxy → public gateway → application-service (save and submit) → Kafka → review-service (officer approves) → Kafka → application-service (marks approved) → Kafka → profile-service (creates the licence) → certificate-service (renders the PDF with its QR) New applications must be paid before an officer sees them. A platform-wide switch chooses between pay-first-review-later and review-first-pay-later, and changing it changes the whole application lifecycle.
A few design choices keep this manageable.
The browser never calls a backend directly. The portal’s own Nitro server proxies every request and turns the httpOnly auth cookie into a Bearer header. Each licence type has a service code and a strategy class. GDTI-RT-L is a new restaurant licence, and adding a licence type means adding strategies rather than growing a switch. Kafka messages go out after the database commits. Business code publishes a Spring domain event, and a transactional listener sends the message after the commit. A rolled-back submission can’t start a review for a row that doesn’t exist. Message schemas live in one repo. Services download their Avro schemas from the Schema Registry at build time, so the producer and the consumer read the same contract. The other operations reuse most of the chain. Renewal runs the editable rule engine and can add a bilingual late-penalty invoice line. Amendment can change the licensee, address and details, but not the capacity band, because the band is the fee. Transfer looks up the recipient’s identity, and termination revokes the existing certificate. Transfer and termination skip the payment gate and go straight to review.
Where the bugs came from When I looked at the defects that reached our dev environment, very few were inside a single service. Most of them sat on a joint between two correct pieces.
A portal called an endpoint that the gateway had no route for. Gateway routes are Java classes, so a forgotten route returns 404 before the service ever sees the request. A producer and a consumer disagreed about an Avro field. I also lost an afternoon to the tenant prefix. The schema publisher adds its own trailing dot, so passing esb. produced subjects named esb..application_submitted_message-value. A seeder inserted duplicate keys, or a fee row lacked a revenue code that the ministry’s workbook listed. A guarded endpoint rejected a user who should have had access. The last case is a good example. Backoffice staff sometimes got a 403 saying they couldn’t view applications from other departments, even in their own department. The portal kept the selected department in a module-level singleton and in a localStorage key that wasn’t tied to any user. Only the explicit Logout button cleared it. After a failed token refresh, the next user inherited the previous user’s department. The backend was right to refuse the request. It had simply received a stale header from the client.
Bringing tests back In October 2026 no test ran in CI, and the Jenkins builds skipped tests. Many test files existed on developers’ machines but had never been committed. When I brought them under version control on 2026-10-19, the baseline was red in 15 of 16 Maven repos and in both portals, and 23 test classes didn’t compile.
We also keep a ledger of deferred defects, and nobody revisits an entry after writing it. I re-checked all 26 open high-severity entries against the current code and databases. Four were already fixed, eleven were confirmed real, and several had a different cause from the one recorded.
The testing strategy we wrote assigns each defect class to the cheapest layer that catches it.
Offline unit tests for each service that run without Schema Registry or Docker. CI can’t run anything until this layer exists. Message-contract checks that reject an incompatible Avro change. Gateway route coverage, so that every portal call has a route. Persistence tests against real Postgres through Testcontainers. Authorization tests for each role and department. What you can take from this If you work on a similar platform, these are the lessons I’d pass on.
Test the joints first. In a multi-repo system, most defects come from two correct pieces disagreeing. Route coverage and contract tests catch more real bugs than extra unit tests. Make the first test layer runnable anywhere. If the build needs a running registry or Docker, CI can’t run the tests, and a test that never runs drifts until it no longer compiles. Re-verify a bug list before you plan from it. An entry records what someone believed on the day they wrote it. Tie client-side context to the user and the session. Any state the client sends as a header must be cleared on every way a session ends, not only the Logout button. Trace one flow end to end before you change anything. I wrote a hop-by-hop trace for a teammate coming from Rails, and it was the most useful document I produced all year. Put policy in configuration. Fees, eligibility rules and penalties change with ministry decisions. When staff can edit them, the platform keeps up with policy without a release.
summary: What I learned building the Ministry of Tourism’s online licensing platform at TSC: what it changes for businesses and the ministry, how one licence moves through five services, and where the bugs actually came from.
title: ESB-MOT: Building Online Tourism Licensing for Cambodia

content:
Background SAAMBAT is a Cambodia-government program supporting agricultural value chains, and KAS is the digital platform behind it. I’ve been working on it at TSC (Techo Startup Center). The platform grew organically over a few years — the kind of growth that ships features but accumulates the usual debts: a Node.js gateway no one fully owned, encryption layered between services that never left the cluster, two separate role tables, and a logging story that depended on whichever engineer set up the service first.
We kicked off a re-engineering program on 2026-01-01 with a clear scope for Phase 1: stop bleeding before adding any new industries. This post is a personal write-up of what shipped between January and the end of April.
The five things that mattered 1. The gateway is now Spring Cloud Gateway The old kas-core was a Node.js proxy doing JWT validation, partner E2EE, and routing. We replaced it with Spring Cloud Gateway on port 3000, with JWT validation moved to the edge using HS256 with a secret shared with kas-iam. Downstream services now verify locally; the /authenticate-jwt round-trip is gone.
Path rewriting is split cleanly: /api/* for internal traffic, /integrations/* for partners. CORS is centralized — localhost only allowed in non-prod profiles, and the Helm chart defaults to the prod Spring profile as a fail-safe.
It’s running in dev. Staging and production are waiting on DevOps to provision the new cluster.
2. We removed internal end-to-end encryption This one took some convincing. The previous design had secp256k1 + AES-256-CBC between every internal service. For traffic that never leaves the cluster, the operational complexity was real and the threat model was thin.
So we ripped it out internally and kept partner-facing E2EE, which we moved out of kas-core and into kas-service-registry — that’s where partner key material already lives. The @kas/e2ee-utils package stays for partner integrations.
Net effect: simpler internal topology, partner trust boundary unchanged.
3. IAM and RBAC, finally consolidated The single biggest defect I personally worked on was a duplicate-roles bug. Migration 001 had created agriculture-scoped roles without removing pre-existing duplicates. The result: createUser validation broke in surprising ways. Migration 003 deduplicates the roles, and createUser now runs Set-based dedup as defense in depth.
Auditing the permission model produced a useful surprise: per-service permission tables were dead data. The frontends drive authorization off roles, not individual permissions. Only USER.* permissions were actually enforced anywhere. So those tables go on the housekeeping pile.
Two smaller fixes in the same pass — the kas-iam Dockerfile now ships the public/ directory (email templates), and EmailController no longer crashes when a template file is missing.
4. Observability — one pattern, every service We picked a single transformation pattern and applied it everywhere:
Winston structured (JSON) logs Correlation IDs end-to-end (HTTP X-Correlation-ID, plus the Socket.io equivalent) Sentry for errors Slack alerting for 5xx with full context ELK for centralized log aggregation All eight backend services are on the pattern. Some are further along on OpenAPI documentation and Vitest coverage than others — kas-iam (43 endpoints), kas-service-registry (13), and kas-weather-api (107) are documented; others still need that pass.
5. Kafka as the event backbone Kafka 3.6, three brokers, KRaft mode (no ZooKeeper). 26 topics across portal, chat, notification, weather, resource, IAM, registry, and DLQ categories. Naming standardized as kas.<service>.<entity>.<event-type>. A kafka-init service auto-creates topics on startup; validate-topics.sh for health checks. Schema Registry 7.5.0 deployed (though contracts are not yet enforced — a known gap). Four DLQ topics in place; replay tooling is still manual, which is on the Phase-2 list. Local development that doesn’t fight you A small thing that mattered a lot: the unified Docker Compose stack in kas-infrastructure/. One command brings up MongoDB replica set, Redis, Kafka cluster, Schema Registry, ELK, and all eight backend services on documented ports. start.sh has --build and --no-cache flags; reset.sh got a --deep.
We also renamed docker-compose.override.yml → docker-compose.staging.yml. The old name was an automatic include — local dev was occasionally pointing at the staging MongoDB by accident. Now staging is opt-in via --staging.
Notable bugs along the way BUG-3 (form-data on kas-resource-api): farmer / family-member submissions were broken. Root cause was formidable 2.1.5 auto-parsing bracket notation while our manual reconstruction code did the same job — they fought. kas-weather-api: form handlers now have a fallback path, and error responses no longer leak internals. What’s left for Phase 1 These are operational, not architectural:
DevOps to provision the new cluster so the gateway can promote dev → staging → production. Once production cuts over, the legacy /authenticate-jwt endpoint can be retired. Housekeeping: sunset kas-core images and CI jobs, drop dead per-service permission tables, remove unused backend routes catalogued in docs/re-architecture/unused-backend-routes.md, scrub kas-core references from service CLAUDE.md files. What we’d need for nation-wide scale Phase 1 got us internally consistent. Going from there to production-grade for a nation-wide rollout is a different list — it’s the one I think about most. The headline items:
Resilience: multi-AZ MongoDB and Kafka, circuit breakers (Resilience4j on the gateway), automated DLQ replay, DR runbooks with documented RTO/RPO. Security: Vault-backed secrets, mTLS between gateway and downstream, rate limiting per principal/route, WAF, PII masking extended beyond kas-iam, a real penetration test, and a Cambodia data-protection compliance review. Observability beyond logs: OpenTelemetry traces, Prometheus + Grafana golden signals, formal SLOs (we have SLA targets but not SLOs), synthetic monitoring from regional vantage points, and an actual on-call rotation rather than Slack-only alerting. Performance: load testing with k6 or Gatling, a capacity plan sized to provinces × users × forms/day, CDN, MongoDB read replicas, Redis cluster mode, a connection-pooling sweep. Data governance: enforce Schema Registry contracts on kas.* topics, adopt one migration tool with idempotency tests, define retention policies, and inventory PII. DX & CI/CD: split CI matrices, contract tests at the gateway boundary, ephemeral pre-merge environments, branch protection and conventional commits, an internal developer portal. Frontend & mobile: offline-first hardening with proven sync conflict handling, low-bandwidth optimizations, Khmer language QA, and WCAG AA for backoffice tools used by government staff. Operational readiness: a real tenant model (province → district → commune as first-class citizens), feature flags for staged regional rollout, bulk import/export tooling for legacy records, training materials, and helpdesk integration. Phase 2, if it happens There’s a proposal on the table to generalize KAS beyond agriculture into a multi-industry data-entry backbone. We’ve done the preparation work — catalogued every place the codebase assumes “agriculture,” drafted the generic submission envelope:
{ "tenantId": "...", "industry": "...", "formId": "...", "schemaVersion": 1, "payload": { }, "attachments": [ ], "geo": { }, "submittedBy": "..." } …and confirmed Schema Registry can host industry-specific payload contracts. The architectural precondition is extracting the form engine out of kas-resource-api into a runtime form-definition service, with industry packs (form definitions + RBAC seed + reference data + optional industry service) as a first-class concept.
But that’s a leadership decision. Engineering’s recommendation is a small, scoped extraction of the form engine first — about a quarter, two or three engineers — before committing to a second industry.
Reflection The most useful thing I learned in Phase 1 isn’t on the report. It’s that picking one transformation pattern and applying it everywhere beats tailoring per-service. The observability rollout went fast precisely because we stopped re-litigating the design at each service. Same for the Docker Compose unification — once the canonical stack existed, every service became “fit into this” rather than “design your own.”
The risk for Phase 2, if leadership greenlights it, isn’t technical. It’s the temptation to keep adding capabilities in parallel with the multi-industry generalization. That’s the way I get a hybrid platform that does neither well. So Phase 2 should ship behind a feature flag, with one new industry as the proof, before anything else.
summary: Notes from four months re-architecting SAAMBAT/KAS at TSC: replacing the gateway, dropping internal E2EE, consolidating IAM, standardizing observability, and putting Kafka in the middle.
title: Re-engineering the KAS Platform — Phase 1
